lead: Sampling turns a continuous signal into numbers taken at fixed instants. It exists because digital storage, PCM speech and software radio cannot carry a continuous waveform directly. If the samples are close enough, the original signal can be rebuilt exactly. If they are too far apart, high frequencies fold down and pretend to be low frequencies, and the damage cannot be undone. This chapter states the sampling theorem, defines the rates, computes aliases, and shows ideal and flat-top reconstruction.
prereq: You need: Fourier transform, bandwidth and spectra from Unit 1; pulse modulation follows in Chapter 4.2.

sections.h3: The theorem and the sample rate

blocks.text: A lowpass signal has no frequency content above fm hertz. The sampling theorem says it can be rebuilt exactly from samples taken at fs ≥ 2fm. Here fs is the sampling rate in samples per second, and fm is the highest message frequency in hertz. The sampling interval is Ts = 1/fs seconds. The Nyquist rate is 2fm samples per second. The Nyquist interval is 1/(2fm) seconds.

Ideal sampling multiplies m(t) by an impulse train with spacing Ts. The sampled spectrum is fs times a sum of shifted copies of the message spectrum. Proof sketch: the impulse train has a spectrum that is also an impulse train at spacing fs; multiplication in time becomes convolution in frequency, so each impulse shifts a copy of M(f) to kfs. If fs ≥ 2fm, the copies occupy separate intervals and an ideal lowpass filter from 0 to fm recovers M(f) exactly. If fs < 2fm, the copies overlap.
s(t) = Σ m(nTs) δ(t − nTs)   and   S(f) = fs Σ M(f − kfs)
blocks.where: s(t) is the ideal sampled signal; m(t) is the message; Ts = 1/fs is the sampling interval in seconds; δ is the unit impulse; S(f) and M(f) are their spectra; fs is the sampling rate; k and n are integers.

blocks.text: A practical sampler is preceded by an anti-alias lowpass filter. It removes noise and interference above fm before sampling, because once folded they cannot be separated from the message. After sampling, a reconstruction lowpass filter removes the replicas. Some syllabi call this the Nyquist–Shannon theorem or the Whittaker theorem.

A tone at f0 above fs/2 does not disappear. Sampling makes it look like a lower tone. The apparent frequency is fa = |f0 − kfs|, with integer k chosen so that 0 ≤ fa ≤ fs/2. Every sampled tone repeats in fs, so f0 and f0 ± fs give the same samples. If f0 is only a little above fs/2, one subtraction is enough. If f0 is much larger, subtract multiples of fs until the result lies in the baseband.

Take fs = 7 kHz with tones at 1 kHz and 4 kHz. The 1 kHz tone is below 3.5 kHz, so it stays at 1 kHz. The 4 kHz tone is above 3.5 kHz; with k = 1, fa = |4 − 7| = 3 kHz. The sampler output therefore contains a 3 kHz component that was not in the input. This folding is aliasing. The figure shows the original lines, the folded line at 3 kHz, and replicas at 6, 8 and 11 kHz.

Prevent aliasing by keeping all input components below fs/2. Put an anti-alias lowpass filter before the sampler. It passes 0 to fm and stops at fs − fm, so noise above fm cannot fold into the message. A guard band between fm and fs − fm allows a real filter with a gradual roll-off. Telephone speech often uses fm ≈ 3.4 kHz and fs = 8 kHz for this reason.

Ideal reconstruction uses sinc interpolation: m(t) = Σ m(nTs) sinc((t − nTs)/Ts). Here sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx), and sinc(0) = 1. Each sample creates a sinc pulse; the sum passes through every sample and has no content above fm. This needs exact sample times and an ideal lowpass filter. Real filters approximate it.

Zero-order hold (ZOH), also called flat-top reconstruction, holds each sample value for Ts seconds. Its response is H(f) = Ts sinc(fTs), apart from a delay. The sinc factor attenuates high frequencies inside the baseband; this is the aperture effect. A compensation filter with a rising response can flatten it. In natural sampling the pulse top follows the message during the pulse. In flat-top sampling the top is flat at the sample value. PAM circuits use both names.

Sampling leads to pulse modulation: PAM varies pulse amplitude, PWM varies width, and PPM varies position; see Chapter 4.2. Bandpass sampling is a separate note. A signal in a band from fL to fH can be sampled below 2fH if the shifted copies do not overlap. Choose fs so the band lands inside 0 to fs/2 without collision. Radio receivers use this to sample a bandpass signal directly.

figure.caption: At fs = 7 kHz the 4 kHz tone folds to 3 kHz, while the 1 kHz tone stays at 1 kHz. The replica lines sit at 6, 8 and 11 kHz.

spec.aria: The plot shows original tones at 1 and 4 kHz, a folded 4 kHz tone at 3 kHz, and sample replicas at 6, 8 and 11 kHz for fs = 7 kHz.

examples.question: A signal m(t) = 3 cos(2π·1000t) + 2 cos(2π·4000t) is sampled at fs = 7000 samples/s. Find the Nyquist rate, decide whether aliasing occurs, and give the alias frequency of the 4 kHz tone. State where the 1 kHz tone appears.
steps: Identify the tones: f1 = 1000 Hz and f2 = 4000 Hz. The highest message frequency is fm = 4000 Hz.
Nyquist rate = 2fm = 2 × 4000 = 8000 samples/s. Nyquist interval = 1/8000 = 0.000125 s = 0.125 ms.
The actual rate is fs = 7000 samples/s. Compare: 7000 < 8000, so fs < 2fm and aliasing occurs.
For the 4 kHz tone, fold with k = 1: fa = |4000 − 7000| = 3000 Hz. This lies between 0 and fs/2 = 3500 Hz, so the alias is 3 kHz.
For the 1 kHz tone, 1000 Hz is below 3500 Hz. It is not folded and appears at 1 kHz.
examples.answer: Nyquist rate = 8000 samples/s; aliasing occurs; the 4 kHz tone appears at 3 kHz, and the 1 kHz tone stays at 1 kHz.
examples.check:
fm = max(1000, 4000)
nyq = 2 * fm
fs = 7000
alias = abs(4000 - fs)
print(fm)
print(nyq)
print(fs)
print(alias)
print(1000)

traps: fs = 2fm is the theoretical limit, not a practical design value. Real anti-alias filters need a guard band, so most systems use fs > 2fm.
The alias must lie in 0 to fs/2. If f0 > fs, subtract multiples of fs; one subtraction can still leave a frequency above fs/2.
Nyquist rate is 2fm samples/s; Nyquist interval is 1/(2fm) seconds. Do not swap them.
The replicas in the sampled spectrum are spaced fs, not fm. Sketch centres at 0, ±fs, ±2fs.
Flat-top sampling is not ideal impulse sampling. Its sinc response droops the baseband; that is the aperture effect, not aliasing.

quiz.q: State the lowpass sampling theorem and define fm, fs and Ts.
quiz.a: A signal with highest frequency fm can be rebuilt exactly if fs ≥ 2fm. fs is samples/s, Ts = 1/fs seconds.

quiz.q: Why is the anti-alias filter placed before the sampler, not after it?
quiz.a: After sampling, aliased components overlap the message and cannot be separated. Before sampling, the filter removes components above fm so they never fold.

quiz.q: A 2.5 kHz tone is sampled at 4 kHz. Find its alias frequency.
A signal is bandlimited to 6 kHz. Find the Nyquist rate and Nyquist interval.
A 9 kHz tone is sampled at 8 kHz. Explain why the output looks like 1 kHz, and state the baseband limit.
quiz.a: fs/2 = 4 kHz. 9 kHz is outside; k = 1 gives |9 − 8| = 1 kHz, inside 0 to 4 kHz. So every sample matches a 1 kHz tone.

quiz.q: Why does flat-top sampling cause aperture effect, and how is it reduced?
quiz.a: Holding each sample for Ts multiplies the spectrum by sinc(fTs), which droops high baseband frequencies. An inverse-sinc compensation filter or a shorter hold reduces it.

quiz.q: m(t) = 5cos(2π·600t) + 2cos(2π·1800t) is sampled at fs = 3000 samples/s. Find Nyquist rate, decide aliasing, and give output frequencies.
quiz.a: fm = 1800 Hz, Nyquist rate = 3600 > 3000, so aliasing. 1800 folds to |1800 − 3000| = 1200 Hz. 600 stays at 600 Hz. Output tones: 600 Hz and 1200 Hz.

beyond: Not for the exam. Software-defined radio uses bandpass sampling to move an RF band directly to a low intermediate frequency. Audio codecs and digital control loops use oversampling and decimation. Search next for bandpass sampling, anti-aliasing filter design, sample-rate conversion, and clock jitter in samplers.
